prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The depth map separates the nearby man, roughly 1–2 m in front of the camera wearer, from the farther walls, windows, doorway, lamp, and plants, which appear about 2–5 m away; it also makes the camera wearer’s very near hand/arm and the pale foreground obstruction—each within roughly 0.2–0.7 m—more obvious than in RGB. Across the five frames, the man shifts from left to center and grows larger, indicating that the camera turns toward him and/or closes the distance to roughly 0.7–1.2 m; his head and torso face generally toward the camera, although exact gaze is obscured by dark glasses. The near hand or pale obstruction intermittently blocks parts of his lower body and the room, while the lamp and other furnishings remain behind and to his right. Absolute metre estimates are uncertain because monocular depth has no reliable scale, and several boundaries—especially the bright foreground obstruction, windows, dark doorway, and the man’s silhouette—show inconsistent or flattened depth.
descriptions.segmentation: The segmentation map cleanly isolates the main man in all five frames, showing him move from the left toward the center and occupy progressively more of the view, consistent with a change from roughly 1–2 m away to about 0.7–1.2 m; the mask shape shows his upper body facing the camera wearer. It also places small room objects mostly behind and to his right, including plant-like objects around 1.5–3 m away, while objects overlapping his lower-right silhouette are likely within his or the camera wearer’s arm’s reach. The map makes occlusion boundaries explicit: a large foreground region covers the man’s lower body in frame 1, and a clipped region at the left edge in frame 5 is partly out of view. Its semantic labels are unreliable—the shirt graphic is detected as “cake,” cups as “bowl” or “bottle,” foliage or a pale plume as “doggy bear,” and foreground regions as additional people—and it provides no direct metric depth, so distances require the RGB and depth map.
descriptions.pose: The pose map tracks facial landmarks and a sparse upper-body skeleton, placing one person left-of-center initially and near the center thereafter; the nearly frontal, roughly symmetric face landmarks indicate that his head generally faces toward the camera wearer, though they cannot establish exact eye gaze. Shoulder width and landmark scale increase slightly across the strip, supporting a modest approach or camera movement from about 1–2 m to around 1 m, while the sloping shoulder lines in frames 2 and 4 indicate changes in upper-body angle or camera roll. In frame 2 both upper arms extend downward and in frame 4 one short arm segment appears at lower right, but the missing hand landmarks prevent reliable judgments about reach or distances to the nearby cup-like objects. The map suppresses all room geometry and objects, misses most limbs and all visible foreground occluders, and occasionally produces detached joints, so it cannot independently describe object layout, occlusion, behind/in-front relationships, or precise inter-person distances.
